title: Microservices Architecture & Service Decomposition
summary: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning one **bounded context** and its own data. The hard part isn't the code — it's drawing the boundaries: too coarse and you have a monolith with network calls, too fine and you drown in operational overhead. In Go this maps cleanly onto `cmd/` binaries, an `internal/` package tree, and transport/domain/store layers. Learn where the seams belong (and when a modular monolith is the right call) before you learn how to wire the RPC.

subtopics.title: Bounded contexts: where the seams go
subtopics.explanation: A bounded context is a slice of the domain with its own consistent language and model — Orders, Inventory, Billing — where the same word ("customer") can mean different things in each. You decompose along these contexts, not along technical layers, so each service owns a coherent business capability. Aligning service boundaries to bounded contexts is the single decision that determines whether your microservices stay loosely coupled or collapse into a distributed monolith.

subtopics.title: Database per service & data ownership
subtopics.explanation: Each service owns its data exclusively and exposes it only through its API — no other service reads or writes its tables. A shared database is the classic anti-pattern: it couples deploy schedules, lets any team break another's schema, and destroys the independence that justified microservices in the first place. Database-per-service is the rule that turns 'services that call each other' into 'services that can actually evolve independently'.

subtopics.title: Sizing services: not too micro
subtopics.explanation: The 'micro' in microservices misleads people into splitting per-entity or per-function, producing dozens of chatty nanoservices that must all be deployed together to do anything useful. A good service is sized to a bounded context and can be owned end-to-end by one team; if two services always change and deploy together, they should be one. Right-sizing keeps the operational cost of a service (its own pipeline, DB, on-call, dashboards) justified by the autonomy it buys.

subtopics.title: Eventual consistency across boundaries
subtopics.explanation: Once data is split across services you can no longer wrap a change in one ACID transaction — you trade strong consistency for eventual consistency, usually via events. When an order is placed, the Order service commits locally and publishes an event; Inventory and Billing react asynchronously and converge over time. Accepting eventual consistency (and designing for the window where services disagree) is the price of data ownership, and it reshapes how every cross-service workflow is written.

subtopics.title: Idiomatic Go service layout
subtopics.explanation: A Go service is typically organized as one binary per service under cmd/, all real code under internal/ (so it can't be imported by other modules), and layers split into transport (HTTP/gRPC), domain (business logic), and store (persistence). The domain layer defines interfaces; transport and store are the adapters that implement them, so business logic never imports net/http or database/sql. This layout makes each service testable in isolation and keeps the bounded context's core independent of its delivery and storage mechanisms.

subtopics.title: Monolith vs microservices: when NOT to
subtopics.explanation: Microservices buy independent deploy, independent scale, and team autonomy — but they cost operational complexity, network failure modes, and painful distributed debugging. If you have one small team, an unclear domain, or no strong deploy/scale pressure, a modular monolith (clean package boundaries in one deployable) gives you most of the design discipline with none of the distributed-systems tax. The mature default is to start monolith-first and extract a service only when a boundary proves itself and a concrete pressure demands it.

foundations.overview: Microservices architecture decomposes an application into a set of small, independently deployable services, each owning a single business capability and its own data store, communicating over the network. The value is not in having many services — it's in the independence: teams can build, deploy, and scale their service without coordinating with everyone else. The catch is that a poorly drawn boundary turns that independence into its opposite: a 'distributed monolith' where services must be deployed together yet suffer all the latency, partial-failure, and debugging pain of a distributed system. The whole discipline is really about drawing the right boundaries — and knowing when a modular monolith is the better answer.
foundations.formalDefinition: A microservice is an independently deployable unit that owns a single bounded context and its private data, exposing its capability only through a well-defined API (HTTP/gRPC/events). A microservices architecture is a system composed of such services communicating over a network, with no shared database and no shared in-memory state, coordinated through APIs and asynchronous events rather than a single process boundary.
foundations.whyItMatters: How you decompose a system determines its long-term velocity: right-sized services let independent teams ship in parallel and scale hot paths separately, while wrong boundaries create cascading deploys, brittle call chains, and consistency bugs. Go's fast startup, small binaries, cheap concurrency, and standard-library networking make it a dominant choice for microservices (Kubernetes, Docker, and most cloud infra are Go services), so decomposition is a core backend and interview skill.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a company reorganizing from one giant open-plan room (the monolith) into separate departments (services), each with its own filing cabinet (database) that no other department may open directly. Departments cooperate by sending memos (API calls and events), not by rummaging in each other's cabinets. Draw the department lines around what the business actually does (Orders, Billing, Inventory) and the org runs smoothly; draw them around job titles or file types and every task needs a meeting with five departments.
foundations.runtimePerspective: At runtime each service is its own OS process (usually its own container/pod), with its own goroutine-per-request server, its own connection pool to its own database, and its own lifecycle (deploy, scale, restart). A single user action may fan out across several processes over the network, so latency compounds, and any hop can fail independently. Cross-service calls carry a context.Context so timeouts and cancellation propagate; asynchronous workflows converge via a message broker rather than a shared transaction.
foundations.realWorldUsage: E-commerce platforms split into Order/Payment/Inventory/Shipping services; streaming and ride-share apps decompose by capability so hot paths scale independently; SaaS platforms give each squad its own service and pipeline. In Go specifically: internal platform services behind an API gateway, gRPC-connected backends, and event-driven pipelines are the bread and butter.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct decomposition lets teams ship features independently and scale expensive paths without over-provisioning the whole system, directly improving time-to-market and cloud cost. Incorrect decomposition does the reverse: coupled deploys slow every release, distributed bugs raise incident rates, and per-service overhead (pipelines, dashboards, on-call) multiplies cost for no autonomy gain.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Service boundaries become team boundaries (Conway's Law), so decomposition shapes ownership, on-call, and how easily teams work in parallel. Good boundaries make each service small, testable, and independently evolvable; bad ones create hidden coupling that surfaces as coordinated releases and cross-team debugging sessions.
foundations.performanceImpact: Splitting a service adds network latency and serialization cost to what used to be an in-process function call, and introduces partial failure, so naive decomposition can make the system slower and less reliable than the monolith it replaced. The upside is targeted scaling: you scale only the hot service (and its DB) instead of the whole app, which is where microservices pay for themselves under uneven load.
commonUseCases: Decomposing a growing monolith by bounded context (Order, Billing, Inventory)
Scaling a hot capability independently of the rest of the system
Giving autonomous teams their own deploy pipeline and on-call surface
Event-driven workflows where services react asynchronously and converge
Isolating a high-risk or compliance-heavy capability (payments) behind its own service and data store

commonMisconceptions.myth: Microservices are always better than a monolith.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For a small team or an unclear domain, a modular monolith ships faster and is far easier to operate. Microservices trade simplicity for autonomy — only worth it under real deploy/scale/team pressure.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Smaller services are always better ('the more micro the better').
commonMisconceptions.reality: Over-splitting creates nanoservices that must deploy together and chatter over the network for a single action — a distributed monolith with worse latency and reliability than the original.

commonMisconceptions.myth: It's fine for two services to share one database to save effort.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A shared DB couples schema changes and deploys across teams and breaks independent evolution — it's the defining anti-pattern that turns microservices back into a monolith with network overhead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can keep strong ACID consistency across services.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Once data is split you lose cross-service transactions; you design for eventual consistency via events/sagas and tolerate a window where services temporarily disagree.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Decomposition is a technical exercise about splitting layers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You decompose along business bounded contexts, not technical layers — splitting by 'controllers/services/repos' gives you a distributed monolith, not autonomous services.

interactiveExamples.title: A single Go service organized by transport / domain / store
interactiveExamples.explanation: This is the canonical shape of one microservice: the domain package defines the business type and a Repository port, the store package is the DB adapter that implements it, and the transport package exposes it over HTTP. Note that the domain (order.Service) never imports net/http or database/sql — dependencies point inward, so the bounded context stays independent of its delivery and storage mechanisms.

code.caption: Dependencies point inward: transport and store depend on the domain's Repository port, never the reverse. This is the layout every Go microservice repeats.

interactiveExamples.title: Cross-service reference by ID, not by shared struct
interactiveExamples.explanation: A common decomposition mistake is sharing rich domain types across service boundaries, which recouples the services. The right pattern is to reference other contexts by opaque ID and fetch only what you need through their API. Here the Order context holds a CustomerID string, not a Customer struct owned by another service — so the two contexts can evolve independently.

code.caption: Reference other contexts by ID and a narrow client interface; never embed another service's domain struct into yours.

interactiveExamples.title: Local commit + event publish (the eventual-consistency seam)
interactiveExamples.explanation: Without a shared database you can't atomically update Order and Billing together, so the Order service commits its own state and emits an event that Billing consumes asynchronously. This example shows the seam: a successful local save is the source of truth, and the published event is what makes the rest of the system eventually converge. In production the publish is made reliable with the outbox pattern so the commit and event can't diverge.

code.caption: Commit local state, then publish the event. Other services react asynchronously — they are eventually consistent, not transactionally consistent, with the order.

checkpoints.prompt: Along what lines should you primarily decompose a system into microservices?
options: One service per developer on the team
checkpoints.explanation: Services should map to bounded contexts — cohesive business capabilities like Order, Billing, Inventory. Splitting by technical layer produces a distributed monolith where a single request hops across layers over the network; splitting per-table or per-developer creates chatty nanoservices with no coherent ownership.

checkpoints.prompt: Two services need customer data, so both open the SAME database and query the customers table directly. Why is this a decomposition anti-pattern?
options: It's fine as long as both use prepared statements
A shared database couples schema/deploys across services, breaking independent evolution
sql.Open is too slow to call from two services
They should share a single *sql.DB variable instead
checkpoints.explanation: Database-per-service is the rule: each service owns its data and exposes it only via its API. A shared table means any schema change by one team can break the other, deploys must be coordinated, and the independence that justified splitting the services is gone. Order should call the Customer service's API instead of reading its table.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the domain layer so it depends on a repository PORT (interface) rather than importing the database directly, keeping the bounded context storage-agnostic.
options: type Repository interface { Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error) }
checkpoints.explanation: The domain defines a Repository interface (the port) and depends only on that; the store package provides the adapter that implements it. This keeps net/http and database/sql out of the business logic so the bounded context can be tested and evolved independently of its storage.

checkpoints.prompt: In this decomposition, Place() saves the order locally and then publishes an event for Billing to consume asynchronously. When Place() returns nil, is Billing guaranteed to have already charged the customer?
options: Yes — publishing the event runs Billing synchronously before return
No — Billing consumes the event asynchronously; consistency is eventual, not immediate
Yes — because there is no error, all services are in sync
No — because Save always fails across services
checkpoints.explanation: Publishing an event only hands it to the broker; Billing consumes it later and updates its own data independently. When Place() returns, the order is committed but Billing may not have charged yet — the system is eventually consistent. Designing for that window (and reliable delivery via an outbox) is inherent to database-per-service decomposition.

codeLab.title: Define a clean service boundary with a port interface
codeLab.instructions: The Order domain must not import the store or transport. Define an `OrderRepository` interface (the port) inside package `order` with a single method `Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)`, and implement `Service.Fetch` so it validates a non-empty id (return an error otherwise) and otherwise delegates to the repository. The domain must depend ONLY on the interface — no database/sql, no net/http.
hints: The port is an interface declared in the domain package; the store implements it elsewhere.
Service should hold the interface type, not *sql.DB — that's what makes it testable with a stub.
Fetch: guard the empty-id case first, then `return s.repo.Get(ctx, id)`.

codeLab.title: Encode the 'should this be a separate service?' decision framework
codeLab.instructions: Implement `ShouldExtract(c Candidate) (bool, string)` that returns whether a capability should become its own service, plus a one-line reason. Recommend extraction ONLY when it is its own bounded context AND (it needs independent scaling OR it is owned by a separate team) AND it does NOT always deploy together with its caller. If it always deploys together, never extract (it's a distributed monolith). If it's not a distinct bounded context, never extract. Return a short reason string in every case.
hints: Reject early: not a bounded context, or always-deploys-together, both mean 'do not extract'.
Only after those guards do you check for a real pressure (scale OR separate team).
Every return path must include a short human-readable reason string.

debuggingLab.title: Two services share one table and a synchronous call chain (distributed monolith)
debuggingLab.symptom: Every 'orders' schema migration breaks the billing service in production, deploys must be released together in lockstep, and a slow Billing call makes the Order API time out even though the order itself was already saved. The team has microservices on paper but zero independence in practice.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two distinct decomposition anti-patterns are stacked here. First, order-service writes directly into billing.invoices — a shared table — so a billing schema change breaks orders and the two services can never deploy independently. Second, Place() makes a synchronous HTTP call to billing inside the request path, so Order's availability is now the product of Billing's availability (a slow or down Billing takes Orders down too), and a failure leaves the system half-committed. Together these turn 'microservices' into a distributed monolith: all the network cost, none of the independence.
commonMistakes: Letting one service read/write another service's tables to 'save an API call'.
Making synchronous cross-service calls in the request hot path for work that could be asynchronous.
Treating cross-service consistency like a local ACID transaction instead of designing for eventual consistency.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Give each service its own data, remove the direct table access, and decouple Billing by committing the order locally and publishing an OrderPlaced event that Billing consumes asynchronously (eventual consistency, made reliable with an outbox).

solution.expectedOutput:
// Order placed and committed independently; billing invoice created
// asynchronously from the OrderPlaced event, each in its own database.

theory.question: What are microservices, and when would you choose a modular monolith over them?
theory.directAnswer: Microservices decompose a system into independently deployable services, each owning a single bounded context and its own data, communicating over the network. You choose them when you have real pressure for independent deploy, independent scaling, or team autonomy that a single deployable can't satisfy. You choose a modular monolith — clean package boundaries in one binary — when you have a small team, an unclear or still-evolving domain, or no strong scale/deploy pressure, because it gives you most of the design discipline (clear seams) without the distributed-systems tax of network failure, operational overhead, and distributed debugging. The mature default is monolith-first, extracting a service only when a boundary proves stable and a concrete pressure demands it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architectural style where the system is a set of network-connected, independently deployable, single-context services with private data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To let independent teams build, deploy, and scale their piece without coordinating with everyone else — trading simplicity for autonomy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each service owns a bounded context and its own DB, exposes an API, and coordinates with others via synchronous calls or asynchronous events rather than a shared process or database.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong point on the monolith-microservices spectrum is one of the most expensive architecture mistakes a team can make, and reasoning about the trade-off is a staple senior-backend interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: Many companies (famously Segment, and Amazon Prime Video's monitoring service) re-consolidated over-split microservices back into a monolith after operational cost outweighed the autonomy benefit.

followUps.question: What's a 'distributed monolith' and why is it the worst outcome?
followUps.answer: Services that must be deployed together and call each other synchronously for a single action — you pay all the network/latency/failure cost of microservices but get none of the independence, making it worse than either a clean monolith or true microservices.

followUps.question: How do you migrate a monolith to microservices safely?
followUps.answer: Extract one proven bounded context at a time (strangler-fig pattern), give it its own database, route traffic incrementally, and only continue when each extraction demonstrably pays off.

theory.question: Explain the 'database per service' rule and why a shared database is an anti-pattern.
theory.directAnswer: Database per service means each service owns its data exclusively and exposes it only through its API — no other service reads or writes its tables or even connects to its database. A shared database is an anti-pattern because it recreates tight coupling: any team's schema change can break another service, deploys must be coordinated, and the independent evolution that justified splitting the services disappears. It also blurs data ownership, so no single service is authoritative for a piece of data. The cost of the rule is that you lose cross-service ACID transactions and must design for eventual consistency (events/sagas), but that price buys the independence that is the entire point of microservices.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The principle that each service is the sole owner of its persistent data and mediates all access to it through its API.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To keep the coupling that a shared schema introduces from leaking back in and re-monolithizing the services.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each service has its own datastore and connection pool; other services get data by calling the owner's API or by consuming events it publishes, never by direct DB access.

theory.whyImportant: Sharing a database is the single most common way teams accidentally build a distributed monolith, so interviewers use it to test whether you understand what actually makes services independent.
theory.realWorldExample: In a Go e-commerce system, the Order service holds an OrderStore over its own Postgres; Billing needs the total, so it consumes an OrderPlaced event rather than SELECTing from the orders table.

followUps.question: How does a service get data it doesn't own?
followUps.answer: By calling the owning service's API synchronously, or (better for decoupling) by subscribing to its events and keeping a local read-model/cache it owns.

followUps.question: How do you keep two services' data consistent without a shared transaction?
followUps.answer: Eventual consistency via events and the outbox pattern (commit + event atomically), or a saga of local transactions with compensating actions on failure.

theory.question: How do you decide service boundaries, and how do bounded contexts and service sizing come into it?
theory.directAnswer: You draw boundaries around bounded contexts from domain-driven design — cohesive business capabilities (Order, Billing, Inventory) that have their own consistent model and language, where the same term can mean different things in different contexts. Size each service to a full bounded context that one team can own end-to-end, not to a single entity or function: over-splitting into nanoservices produces chatty synchronous call chains and coupled deploys (a distributed monolith), while under-splitting recreates the monolith. A practical test: if two candidate services always change and deploy together, they belong in one service; and things that reference each other should do so by ID across the boundary, not by sharing rich domain structs. Boundaries also become team boundaries (Conway's Law), so they must fit the org.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The practice of aligning each service to a DDD bounded context sized for single-team ownership and independent deploy.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because coupling and cohesion — not lines of code — determine the right size, and bounded contexts are where the natural low-coupling seams lie.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Identify contexts by language and ownership, reference across contexts by ID, and validate a boundary by whether the two sides can deploy and scale independently.

theory.whyImportant: Boundary drawing is the decision that makes or breaks a microservices architecture, and it's the hardest, least mechanical part — exactly why interviewers probe it.
theory.realWorldExample: Splitting a shopping app into Catalog, Cart, Order, and Payment contexts (each with its own DB and team) rather than into Product-, Price-, Tax-, and LineItem-services that must all be called to place one order.

followUps.question: What signals tell you a boundary is wrong?
followUps.answer: Chatty synchronous calls for a single user action, coordinated lockstep deploys, shared database tables, and cross-team debugging sessions for one feature.

followUps.question: How does Conway's Law affect decomposition?
followUps.answer: Systems mirror the communication structure of the org that builds them, so service boundaries should align with team boundaries — otherwise you fight the org structure constantly.

scenario.question: A 4-person startup with an unproven product wants to launch with 12 microservices 'to be scalable from day one'. What do you advise and why?
scenario.directAnswer: Advise against it: start with a modular monolith and extract services later. With 4 people and an unproven domain, the boundaries are still guesses, and getting them wrong in 12 separate deployables is enormously expensive to correct — you'd be paying 12 pipelines, 12 databases, 12 on-call surfaces, plus network failure and distributed-debugging overhead, all before you have product-market fit. Instead, build one binary with clean internal package boundaries per bounded context (internal/order, internal/billing) communicating through interfaces in-process. That preserves the design discipline and makes each context easy to extract into a service later, once a boundary has proven stable and a concrete scale or team-autonomy pressure appears. Optimize for changing your mind cheaply, not for a scale you don't yet have.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A monolith-first strategy that keeps clean seams so services can be extracted when justified.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because premature decomposition locks in boundary guesses that are cheap to change inside one binary and very expensive to change across many services.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Bounded contexts live as packages behind interfaces in one deployable; extraction happens along an existing interface seam when pressure demands it.

scenario.whyImportant: Premature microservices is a classic startup-killer, and recognizing it demonstrates architectural judgment over hype-driven design.
scenario.realWorldExample: Teams that split too early (e.g., early-stage startups mimicking Netflix) routinely spend months re-merging services; monolith-first teams extract only the one or two services that actually needed it.

followUps.question: What would make you actually extract a service later?
followUps.answer: A proven-stable boundary plus a concrete pressure: a hot path that must scale independently, a team that needs its own deploy cadence, or a compliance domain (payments) you want isolated.

followUps.question: How do you keep a monolith from rotting into a big ball of mud?
followUps.answer: Enforce package boundaries and dependency direction (internal/, interfaces as ports), forbid cross-context DB access, and treat each context's public interface as a contract.

scenario.question: Your Order and Inventory services share one Postgres database and every Inventory migration causes Order outages. How do you decouple them?
scenario.directAnswer: The root cause is a shared database that couples the two services' schemas and deploys. Decouple by giving each service its own database and eliminating all cross-service table access: Inventory becomes the sole owner of its stock tables, and Order must get inventory data through Inventory's API or via events instead of SELECTing its tables. Migrate incrementally — carve the inventory tables into a separate datastore behind Inventory's API, switch Order to call that API/consume events, then physically separate the databases. Replace any synchronous inventory checks in the order hot path with an asynchronous reservation flow where feasible (Order publishes OrderPlaced, Inventory reserves and emits StockReserved/StockRejected), accepting eventual consistency. Once separated, an Inventory migration can never touch Order's schema, and each can deploy on its own cadence.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A decoupling migration that restores database-per-service ownership and removes cross-service DB access.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because a shared database is the coupling that makes independent deploys impossible; removing it is the only real fix.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Split the datastore, mediate all access through the owner's API/events, and move to eventual consistency for cross-service workflows.

scenario.whyImportant: Shared-database coupling is one of the most common real production pain points in microservices, and the fix demonstrates you understand data ownership, not just service splitting.
scenario.realWorldExample: A Go order platform moved inventory into its own service+DB and switched from SELECTing stock to an event-driven reservation (OrderPlaced -> StockReserved), ending the cross-service migration outages.

followUps.question: How do you handle the transition period when both still read the old table?
followUps.answer: Use the strangler-fig pattern: route reads through the new Inventory API while dual-writing/backfilling, then cut over and drop Order's direct access once traffic is fully migrated.

followUps.question: What if Order truly needs a synchronous stock check at checkout?
followUps.answer: Keep a narrow synchronous Inventory API for that specific check with a tight timeout, circuit breaker, and fallback, but move everything else to asynchronous events to minimize the coupling.

systemDesign.question: Design the service decomposition for an e-commerce checkout in Go. Identify the services, their data ownership, and how they stay consistent.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Decompose along bounded contexts: an Order service (owns orders), a Payment service (owns transactions), an Inventory service (owns stock), and a Notification service (owns delivery of messages), fronted by an API gateway. Each is its own Go binary (cmd/server) with internal/ transport/domain/store layers and its OWN database — no shared tables. Checkout works as a saga: Order commits the order locally and publishes OrderPlaced; Inventory consumes it, reserves stock, and emits StockReserved or StockRejected; Payment charges and emits PaymentSucceeded/Failed; on any failure, compensating events (ReleaseStock, CancelOrder) unwind the workflow. Consistency is eventual, coordinated by events through a broker, with the outbox pattern so each service's local commit and its published event are atomic. Synchronous calls are reserved for read paths that genuinely need immediate answers (a stock check), wrapped with context timeouts, retries, and a circuit breaker; everything else is asynchronous to keep services independently available.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A context-aligned set of independently deployable Go services coordinated by events, each owning its own data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So each capability (order, payment, inventory) can be built, scaled, and deployed by its team without shared-DB coupling.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A saga of local transactions plus events drives the cross-service checkout; the outbox guarantees commit/event atomicity; the gateway and per-service APIs mediate access.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Checkout is the canonical decomposition interview because it forces you to reason about boundaries, data ownership, and consistency without a distributed transaction.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: Large Go-based commerce backends run exactly this shape: separate Order/Payment/Inventory services with their own datastores, coordinated by Kafka/NATS events and sagas.

followUps.question: Why a saga instead of a two-phase commit across services?
followUps.answer: 2PC couples availability (all participants must be up and locked) and scales poorly; a saga of local transactions with compensations keeps each service independently available and is the standard microservices approach.

followUps.question: How do you keep the event and the local DB write atomic?
followUps.answer: The outbox pattern: write the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, then a relay publishes it to the broker, so the commit and the event can never diverge.

systemDesign.question: How would you lay out a single Go microservice repository, and how does that structure support decomposition and independent deploy?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Lay it out as one module per service: cmd/server/main.go holds the tiny wiring/entry point; internal/ holds all real code so no other module can import it; and inside internal/ split by layer — transport (HTTP/gRPC handlers), domain (entities, business rules, and the port interfaces it needs), and store (the DB adapter implementing those ports). Dependencies point inward: transport and store depend on domain, never the reverse, so the business logic imports neither net/http nor database/sql. This supports decomposition because the domain is a self-contained bounded context testable in isolation with stub adapters, and independent deploy because each service is its own module, binary, database, and pipeline. When a boundary must be extracted from a monolith, the domain's port interface is precisely the seam you cut along; when you scale, you scale this one binary and its DB without touching others.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The cmd/internal + transport/domain/store layout that is standard for a Go service.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To keep the bounded context's core independent of delivery and storage so it stays testable and independently deployable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The domain defines ports (interfaces); transport and store are adapters wired together in cmd/server via dependency injection, with dependencies pointing inward.

systemDesign.whyImportant: This layout is the concrete, in-code expression of clean boundaries and is what interviewers expect a Go engineer to reach for when asked to structure a service.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: The widely used golang-standards project-layout and most production Go services follow cmd/ + internal/ with transport/domain/store (or handler/service/repository) separation.

followUps.question: Why put code under internal/?
followUps.answer: The Go compiler forbids importing internal/ packages from outside the module, enforcing the service boundary so other teams/services can't reach into your implementation.

followUps.question: Where do the port interfaces live, domain or store?
followUps.answer: In the domain (the consumer defines the interface it needs); the store package provides the concrete adapter — this keeps dependencies pointing inward toward the domain.

coding.question: Implement a decision helper `ShouldExtract(c Candidate) (bool, string)` that encodes when a capability should become its own microservice, returning a recommendation and a reason. Extract only when it is a distinct bounded context AND (needs independent scaling OR is owned by a separate team) AND does NOT always deploy with its caller.
coding.thoughtProcess: Encode the decision framework as guard clauses so the disqualifiers are checked first and the reason is specific. If it isn't a distinct bounded context, never extract. If it always deploys with its caller, extracting produces a distributed monolith — never extract. Only after those guards do we require a real pressure: independent scaling or separate-team ownership. If neither pressure exists, a package/module is cheaper than a service. Return a human-readable reason on every path so the recommendation is explainable.
coding.lineByLine: Candidate captures the four signals that drive the decision. ShouldExtract checks disqualifiers first: a non-context is never a service, and a capability that always deploys with its caller would become a distributed monolith if split, so both return false with a specific reason. Only after passing those guards do we require at least one genuine pressure — independent scaling or separate-team ownership; if neither is present, an in-process module is cheaper and we decline. If every condition is satisfied we recommend extraction with an explaining reason, so the output is auditable rather than a bare boolean.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a fixed sequence of boolean checks.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — no allocation beyond the returned reason string.

followUps.question: How would you extend this to score partial cases instead of a hard yes/no?
followUps.answer: Assign weights to each signal (context, scale, team, coupling penalty) and return a score with a threshold, so borderline candidates surface for human review rather than a binary decision.

followUps.question: Why check AlwaysDeploysWithCaller before checking the pressures?
followUps.answer: Because deploy-coupling is a hard disqualifier: even a hot, separately-owned context becomes a distributed monolith if it must ship in lockstep, so it must veto extraction regardless of the pressures.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Align each service to a bounded context, give it its own database, and expose it only through a well-defined API (HTTP/gRPC) plus events. Structure every service as cmd/ (entry point) + internal/ with transport/domain/store layers, dependencies pointing inward. Prefer asynchronous events for cross-service workflows and reserve synchronous calls for read paths that truly need an immediate answer. Front the fleet with an API gateway and keep a service registry / DNS for discovery. Default to monolith-first and extract along proven interface seams.
productionDeepDive.performance: Every extracted boundary converts an in-process call into a network round-trip, so watch fan-out: a single user action that triggers a synchronous chain of N services multiplies latency and failure probability. Use gRPC (binary, HTTP/2 multiplexing) for internal hops, reuse a tuned http.Client/gRPC connection with pooling, batch where possible, and cache read-models a service owns rather than re-fetching. Scale only the hot service and its DB independently — the whole reason to decompose.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Each service is a goroutine-per-request server, so its handlers must treat shared state as concurrent and propagate r.Context() into every downstream call so client disconnects and timeouts cancel work across the hop. Bound cross-service fan-out with errgroup/semaphores, and make event consumers idempotent because at-least-once delivery means the same event can arrive twice. Never assume a cross-service workflow is atomic.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Design for partial failure: every synchronous cross-service call gets a context timeout, bounded jittered retries, and a circuit breaker so a slow dependency can't cascade. Use the saga pattern with compensating actions instead of distributed transactions, and the outbox pattern so a local commit and its published event can't diverge. Make consumers idempotent, add dead-letter queues, and set per-service SLOs so one service's degradation is contained.
productionDeepDive.observability: Distributed debugging is the tax of decomposition, so invest early: propagate a trace/request ID through context and across every hop, adopt OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing, emit structured logs with the trace ID, and record RED metrics (Rate/Errors/Duration) per service and per route. A single trace spanning Order -> Inventory -> Payment is what makes a cross-service latency spike diagnosable at all.
productionDeepDive.security: Authenticate and authorize at the gateway and re-verify inside services (zero trust between services), use mTLS for service-to-service traffic, and scope each service's DB credentials to only its own data (enforcing ownership at the infra layer). Validate and size-limit inputs at every boundary, never let a service reach another's database, and keep secrets per-service so a compromise is contained.

caseStudies.problem: A serverless, highly-distributed audio/video monitoring pipeline hit scaling limits and high orchestration cost from too many fine-grained components.
caseStudies.solution: They consolidated the over-distributed components back into a single, more monolithic service.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Gave up some independent scaling of individual steps in exchange for far lower orchestration overhead and cost, and simpler operation.
caseStudies.lessons: Microservices are not universally superior; over-decomposition can cost more than it saves, and consolidating is a legitimate, mature decision.

caseStudies.problem: An explosion of microservices (one per destination) created enormous operational overhead — hundreds of repos, pipelines, and shared library versions to keep in sync.
caseStudies.solution: They re-consolidated the fleet back into a monolith to regain manageable operations.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Lost fine-grained independent deploy per destination, but drastically reduced operational and dependency-management burden.
caseStudies.lessons: Right-size services to what a team can operate; per-entity nanoservices multiply overhead without proportional autonomy, and a monolith can be the correct answer.

keyTakeaways: Microservices are independently deployable services each owning one bounded context and its own data; the value is autonomy (independent deploy/scale/team), not the number of services.

Decompose along DDD bounded contexts and business capabilities, not technical layers, and size each service so one team can own it end-to-end — over-splitting yields chatty nanoservices, under-splitting recreates the monolith.

Database per service is the defining rule: each service owns its data and exposes it only via its API; a shared database is the anti-pattern that recreates coupling and destroys independent evolution.
Splitting data means giving up cross-service ACID transactions — design for eventual consistency with events, sagas, and the outbox pattern, and make consumers idempotent.

The trade-off is autonomy vs. operational complexity, network failure, and distributed debugging; a modular monolith is often the better default, so start monolith-first and extract a service only when a boundary proves itself under real pressure.

A Go service is laid out as cmd/ + internal/ with transport/domain/store layers and dependencies pointing inward, so the bounded context stays testable and its port interfaces are the seams you extract along.
